content: The shorter treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) includes a combination of bedaquiline, linezolid (administered for 2 months), levofloxacin, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. This regimen is designed to be completed within 9 to 12 months. No comparator group was included in the study evaluating this regimen. Treatment outcomes assessed included treatment success, treatment completion, failure, relapse, and death. Post-treatment outcomes, such as death and relapse, were evaluated using programmatic data and mortality registries. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, specifically Module 4 for drug-resistant TB, were updated in 2022. These guidelines incorporate data from multiple cohorts, including the 2021 WHO Individual Patient Data (IPD) analysis, which confirmed rifampicin resistance through molecular or culture-based drug susceptibility testing. The IPD data served as an external comparator for evaluating treatment regimens. Participants in the study received either a 9–12 month all-oral regimen containing at least bedaquiline and linezolid or a WHO-recommended bedaquiline-containing all-oral regimen from 2019. This regimen included 4–6 months of bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, and ethionamide, followed by 5 months of levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Alternatively, participants could receive a longer all-oral treatment regimen lasting 18 months or more, which also included bedaquiline and linezolid. The NExT trial, conducted in South Africa, evaluated a 6–9 month regimen consisting of linezolid, bedaquiline, levofloxacin, pyrazinamide, ethionamide/high-dose isoniazid, and terizidone. This regimen was compared to a 21–24 month regimen that included kanamycin, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, ethionamide/high-dose isoniazid, and terizidone. Treatment success was defined as cure or treatment completion without relapse, assessed 24 months after treatment initiation. The TB-PRACTECAL trial was a multi-center, open-label, randomized controlled Phase 2/3 trial evaluating 24-week all-oral regimens for biologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB (RR/MDR-TB). The regimens included combinations of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin or clofazimine. Stage 1 of the trial focused on safety and preliminary efficacy, while Stage 2 evaluated the safety and efficacy of three investigational regimens compared to the standard of care at 72 weeks post-randomization. The primary efficacy outcome was the composite endpoint of unfavorable outcomes (failure, death, treatment discontinuation, recurrence, or loss to follow-up) at 72 weeks. Secondary outcomes included culture conversion rates, serious adverse events, and recurrence rates. Eligibility criteria for the TB-PRACTECAL trial included individuals aged 15 and older with microbiological confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum and resistance to at least rifampicin. Participants were randomized into one of three investigational arms or the standard of care arm. The investigational regimens were as follows: Arm 1: 24 weeks of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin (BPaLM). Arm 2: 24 weeks of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and clofazimine (BPaLC). Arm 3: 24 weeks of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL). The trial was terminated early in March 2021 based on a recommendation from the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB). Interim analysis showed a significant difference favoring the BPaLM regimen (Arm 1) over the standard of care for the primary outcome, driven by a higher rate of treatment discontinuation in the control arm. No treatment failures or recurrences were reported, and five deaths occurred in the control arm compared to none in the BPaLM arm. The South African National TB Program introduced a 9–12 month bedaquiline-based oral regimen in 2017, replacing injectable-based regimens. This regimen included bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. Eligibility criteria included no prior exposure to second-line drugs for more than one month and susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and injectables. Patients not meeting these criteria received an 18–24 month bedaquiline-containing regimen. In 2019, the South African program transitioned to a modified 9–12 month regimen that replaced ethionamide with linezolid for the first 2 months. This change was due to ethionamide’s association with resistance and adverse effects such as nausea and vomiting. Patients with poor prognostic factors, such as extensive disease or prior second-line drug exposure, received longer regimens lasting 18–24 months. Follow-up data for South African cohorts were obtained through the Electronic Drug-Resistant TB Register (EDRWeb) and routine mortality reporting. Relapse and post-treatment deaths were identified using unique patient identifiers. Data included demographics, treatment history, HIV status, drug resistance testing, and treatment outcomes. Statistical analyses accounted for changes in comparator regimens over time and the early termination of the TB-PRACTECAL trial.
